report.releaseDate: 26 Oct 2026 (Q3-26 Destatis/BMF cash tax data; GGL Marktmonitor Q2-26 and Tätigkeitsbericht 2025 as market base)
report.currency: EUR (tables in € millions unless stated; ~USD at an ASSUMED EUR/USD 1.17 — see confidence note)
report.verdict: Germany's Q3-26 gambling tax take rose 11% YoY to €622.1m (~$728m), but the shape — July +26%, August +12.5%, September implied ~−3% — says this is a World Cup timing effect on a 5.3%-of-stakes tax, not a step-change in underlying demand. The regulated market is large (€14.4bn GGR in 2025, flat) yet only ~24% online, with online growth (stakes +9–10% in H1-26) bought under a turnover-tax and €1-stake regime that compresses margins and leaks 23–80% of casino play offshore depending on whose study you believe. The GlüStV 2021 evaluation due 31 Dec 2026 and the 2027 licence-renewal cycle are the swing factors for anyone deciding to enter.

kpis.label: Online channelisation (legal share of online stakes)

summary: **Headline: gambling tax +11% in Q3-26.** Cash receipts of the Rennwett- und Lotteriesteuer family (lottery tax, sports betting tax, virtual slot tax, online poker tax, horse-race betting tax — federal law, revenue accrues to the Länder) reached €622.1m (~$728m) in Jul–Sep 2026 vs ~€560.5m (~$656m) a year earlier, +€61.6m (~$72m). Corroborated across Gaming Intelligence and Mundovideo, both citing Destatis/BMF cash data.

**The monthly shape is a World Cup artefact, not a trend break.** BMF monthly data: July €209m (~$245m, +26%), August €219m (~$256m, +12.5%); September is therefore implied at ~€194m (~$227m), roughly −3% YoY (derived from rounded figures). The 5.3% stake taxes are filed monthly on the prior month's stakes, so July cash largely captures June World Cup 2026 betting (tournament 11 Jun–19 Jul). Underlying ex-event growth is low-to-mid single digit.

**9M-26 tax €1,901m (~$2.22bn), ~+4% YoY implied.** Q1 €632.3m (~$740m, slightly down YoY per trade press), Q2 €647.0m (~$757m), Q3 €622.1m. BMF reported Jan–Aug at €1,708m (~$2.00bn, +5.2%). FY-25 was €2.46bn (~$2.88bn, −1%) after €2.48bn in FY-24; the official BMF 2026 estimate of €2,510m (~$2.94bn, +1.9%) now looks conservative — Q4 need only reach ~€609m (−4% YoY) to hit it.

**Tax base is TURNOVER, not GGR — the defining economic feature.** RennwLottG (as amended 2021): sports betting 5.3% of stakes; virtual slots 5.3% of stakes; online poker 5.3% of stakes; horse-race betting 5.3% of stakes; lotteries 20% of ticket price net of tax (≈16.7% of gross ticket). At the 2025 virtual-slot hold of 11.8% this equates to ~45% of GGR; at the reported 22.8% sports-betting hold it is ~23% of GGR. Online casino table games (Land-level), Spielbanken (Land casino levy) and gaming halls (municipal amusement tax + VAT) sit outside this line.

**Lottery dominates the tax line.** Applying 5.3% to GGL-reported stakes gives ~€204m (Q1-26) and ~€192m (Q2-26) from sports/slots/poker/horse; the residual ~€429m (~$502m) and ~€455m (~$532m) — ~68–70% of receipts — is lottery tax (derived estimate; Destatis product split not available in sources read).

**Market size: €14.4bn (~$16.8bn) GGR in 2025, flat YoY** (GGL Tätigkeitsbericht 2025, relayed). Land-based €10.9bn (~$12.8bn, ~75%); online €3.5bn (~$4.1bn, +2%) — online penetration ~24%, low for a large Western European market. All gambling taxes and levies (incl. Spielbankabgabe, lottery concession levies) totalled €6.9bn (~$8.1bn, −1%), of which licensed operators' RennwLottG contribution was €2.46bn (−1%).

**Online product mix (2025 GGR).** Sports betting €1.89bn (~$2.21bn, −4%) on €8.3bn (~$9.7bn) stakes, football 77% of activity, live betting 53% of wagers; virtual slots €543m (~$635m, +11%) on €4.6bn (~$5.4bn) stakes; online poker rake €69m (~$81m, −0.7%); online horse betting €19m (~$22m, +5%); social lotteries €807m (~$944m), online portion €444m (~$519m, +11%).

**2026 stakes momentum is stronger than 2025 GGR suggests.** GGL Marktmonitor: Q1-26 stakes €3,842m (~$4.50bn, +9.4% vs €3,513m), online €3,220m (84%, +10.0%); Q2-26 €3,624m (~$4.24bn), online €3,111m (86%). H1-26 ≈ €7,466m (~$8.7bn). Sports betting Q1 €2,431m (+11.6%), slots €1,201m (+9.3%), poker €186m (−11.4%), online horse €23m.

**Retail sports betting is a shrinking niche.** Retail stakes fell from €622m (~$728m) in Q1-26 to €512m (~$599m) in Q2-26, i.e. 25.6% → 23.0% of sports stakes; online sports stakes €1,809m → €1,711m. Retail shops are Land-licensed with distance rules and carry the same 5.3% stake tax.

**Licensing regime: GlüStV 2021 + GGL.** The Interstate Treaty (in force 1 Jul 2021) centralised online licensing in the Gemeinsame Glücksspielbehörde der Länder (Halle/Saale; full competence since 1 Jan 2023). Licence types: sports betting (online/retail), virtual slots, online poker, online lottery brokerage, social/class lotteries; online table games are reserved to each Land (Schleswig-Holstein live; NRW process [unverified]). Security deposit €5m (~$5.9m), scalable to €50m (~$58.5m) [statutory, from analyst reference]. In 2025 LUGAS processed data from >60 licensed operators and ~5m registered player accounts.

**Product and player-protection constraints are the tightest in Western Europe.** €1 (~$1.17) maximum stake per spin, ≥5-second spin, no autoplay, no jackpots, no live casino under the federal regime; €1,000 (~$1,170)/month cross-operator deposit cap enforced through LUGAS limit and activity files (no parallel play); OASIS self-exclusion; panic button; 06:00–21:00 broadcast/online ad ban for slots and poker; no sports-betting ads with active athletes or during live broadcasts [GlüStV §§5–8, 22a from analyst reference].

**Channelisation is contested and vertical-specific.** A study reported 16 Mar 2026 put legal share at 77.03% / unlicensed 22.97% of online play; industry associations count 382 German-language illegal sites against 34 licensed platforms and cite 70–80% offshore leakage in casino/slots. GGL enforcement 2025: 2,662 illegal gambling/advertising sites reviewed, 1,843 (69%) taken down. The turnover tax and €1 stake cap are the structural cause.

**Operator landscape — no official share data.** GGL does not publish operator shares. Principal licensed brands (analyst reference, shares n/a): sports — Tipico (market leader), bet365, bwin (Entain), Betano, Interwetten, Admiral (Novomatic), Merkur Bets (Gauselmann), Betway, Winamax; slots — Merkur, Löwen Play, Tipico Games, bwin, LeoVegas, Wildz; lottery brokerage — ZEAL (Lotto24/Tipp24; 9M-26 revenue near €200m per trade press), Lottoland; state lotteries via the 16-member Deutscher Lotto- und Totoblock (monopoly).

**Payments: bank-rail market, no crypto.** Licensed sites run on SEPA transfer, Sofort/Klarna, PayPal, paysafecard and cards; crypto and credit extension are not permitted; the GGL can order payment-service providers to block flows to unlicensed operators (§9 GlüStV). Deposit caps and KYC at registration make payment friction a conversion cost versus offshore sites [regime description, not quantified].

**Political direction: evaluation, then slow consensus.** §32 GlüStV requires the Länder to evaluate the treaty by 31 Dec 2026; the treaty runs to 31 Dec 2028 with automatic extension unless terminated [analyst reference]. Any amendment needs all 16 Landtage. Live agenda: stake/deposit limits, live-betting scope, nationwide table-game licences, tax base (industry lobbies for GGR), enforcement against offshore, and player-reimbursement litigation for the pre-2021 period (BGH/CJEU track; status [unverified]). Christian Hochgrebe chairs the GGL Administrative Board since 1 Jul 2026.

**Fiscal dependence anchors conservatism.** The state took €6.9bn in gambling taxes and levies in 2025 — mostly lottery and Spielbank levies — which protects the Lotto monopoly and makes the Länder reluctant to trade a reliable turnover tax for a GGR tax that would favour operators.

**Read-through for B2Tech.** Germany is a large, stable, lottery-heavy market where the addressable online pool for a private operator (sports + slots + poker) is ~€2.5bn GGR and growing low-to-mid single digits in GGR, high single digits in stakes. Economics are gated by the 5.3% stake tax and marketing restrictions, so scale, pricing discipline and low bonus intensity matter more than acquisition spend; a B2B supply model (GGL-compliant content/platform to licensed operators) carries less regulatory beta than B2C entry. Time any B2C move to the 2027 licence-renewal window and the post-evaluation rule-set.

segments.name: Sports betting (online & retail)
segments.headline: Largest private vertical (€1.89bn GGR 2025, −4%) with stakes re-accelerating in 2026 (+11.6% Q1) and a World Cup bump in Q3 tax; 5.3% stake tax equals ~23% of GGR at the reported hold.
narrative: Sports betting is the anchor of the GGL-licensed market. In 2025 the GGL reported stakes of €8.3bn (~$9.7bn) and gross gaming revenue of €1.89bn (~$2.21bn), down 4% in a year without a major summer tournament; football accounted for 77% of activity and live (in-play) betting for 53% of wagers. The implied hold of 22.8% is well above the 15–20% typical of mature European books; the GGL's Bruttospielertrag definition (stakes minus winnings, before bonus cost, with the 5.3% tax commonly deducted from player stakes or winnings) likely inflates the figure relative to operator-reported net gaming revenue, so treat it as an upper bound rather than an operating margin [interpretation, unverified].

The 2026 quarterly Marktmonitor shows demand re-accelerating. Q1-26 sports stakes were €2,431m (~$2.84bn), +11.6% on €2,179m, split €1,809m online and €622m retail; Q2-26 was €2,223m (~$2.60bn), split €1,711m online and €512m retail. Retail's share slipped from 25.6% to 23.0% in a single quarter — the structural migration continues and is reinforced by Land-level shop licensing with minimum-distance rules. Q3-26 stakes are not yet published (the GGL Marktmonitor typically lags six to eight weeks), but the tax line is instructive: July receipts of €209m (+26%) across all RennwLottG taxes imply a sharp June/early-July surge, consistent with the FIFA World Cup 2026 (11 Jun–19 Jul). Had the full +€61.6m Q3 tax delta come from sports betting alone it would imply ~+€1.2bn of incremental stakes (+~50%); the true figure is lower because slots (+9–10%) and lottery jackpots also contributed, so the sports-betting Q3 uplift is best read as strong double-digit but unquantified.

Tax economics dominate the P&L. The Sportwettensteuer is 5.3% of stakes regardless of licence status and regardless of margin — a losing month still pays. Derived receipts are ~€129m (~$151m) for Q1-26 and ~€118m (~$138m) for Q2-26 (5.3% × GGL stakes), i.e. ~€450–500m annualised (estimate; Destatis product split not retrieved). At an 18% net hold the tax is ~29% of GGR; at 23% it is ~23%. Combined with the ban on advertising with active athletes and on in-play advertising during live broadcasts, and the live-betting catalogue restrictions (final result and next-event markets, as specified by the GGL) [analyst reference], the regime rewards incumbents with brand recall — Tipico, bet365, bwin, Betano, Interwetten — and penalises bonus-led acquisition.

Channelisation in sports betting is materially better than in casino because the tax applies to every bet taken from Germany, licensed brands dominate search and sponsorship, and the product gap to offshore (odds, live markets) is narrower than the slot gap. The commercial implication for an entrant is that sports betting is the credible front door to the market — but only with differentiated pricing or live content, a lean cost base, and a retail strategy limited to selective Länder; retail at 23% of stakes and falling is not where to deploy capital.

Guidance and outlook: the GGL does not guide. Our estimate is sports-betting stakes of €9.0–9.3bn for FY-26 (+8–12%) on World Cup and online migration, GGR growth below that if hold normalises after an operator-friendly tournament; the Q4 Bundesliga/Champions League schedule and the absence of a major tournament in 2027 point to mid-single-digit stake growth next year (estimate).

segments.name: Online casino: virtual slots, poker and table games
segments.headline: Slots are the growth engine (GGR +11% to €543m in 2025; stakes +9% in 2026) but a 5.3% turnover tax at 11.8% hold is ~45% of GGR, poker is shrinking (stakes −11%), and table games remain Land-fragmented.
narrative: Virtual slot machines are the only large online vertical growing double-digit. GGL 2025 figures (relayed) show GGR of €543m (~$635m), +€53m or +11% YoY, on stakes of €4.6bn (~$5.4bn) — an implied hold of 11.8%, which is what you get when the €1 per-spin cap and ≥5-second spin force low-volatility, ~88–90% RTP games. Momentum has held in 2026: Q1 stakes €1,201m (~$1.41bn, +9.3% on €1,099m) and Q2 €1,214m (~$1.42bn), the only product to grow sequentially into the seasonally weaker second quarter. Annualised Q2 stakes of ~€4.9bn point to FY-26 slots GGR of ~€570–590m (estimate) if hold is stable.

Online poker is in structural decline inside the regulated perimeter: 2025 rake €69m (~$81m, −0.7%), Q1-26 stakes €186m (~$218m, −11.4% on €210m), Q2-26 €158m (~$185m). The 5.3% tax on stakes (buy-ins) and the prohibition on cross-border liquidity make licensed poker uncompetitive with offshore pools; it is a retention product for sportsbook/slots operators, not a standalone opportunity.

Tax arithmetic is the central problem. Derived receipts are ~€64m (~$75m) per quarter for slots and ~€8–10m for poker (5.3% × stakes), roughly €290m annualised (estimate). Relative to GGR, the slots levy is ~45% — higher than any GGR-based online casino tax in Western Europe — and it is payable irrespective of bonus cost, so effective tax on net revenue after promotions is higher still. This is why the regulated offer (€1 stake, no jackpots, no autoplay, no live dealer, €1,000/month cross-operator deposit cap via LUGAS, no parallel play) co-exists with a large offshore market: the study reported 16 Mar 2026 put unlicensed share at 22.97% of all online play, while industry associations argue 70–80% of casino/slot activity sits offshore and count 382 German-language illegal sites against 34 licensed platforms. Both can be true — channelisation is high in sports betting and low in casino.

Table games (roulette, blackjack, live casino) are not federally licensed. Under GlüStV §22c each Land may license online table games, capped at the number of its land-based Spielbank concessions; Schleswig-Holstein operates its own regime and North Rhine-Westphalia has moved to license a limited number of operators [status unverified in this session]. Nationwide, therefore, the only legal online 'casino' product for a B2C entrant is virtual slots plus poker, and the table-games opportunity is a Land-by-Land tender game with small prize pools.

Enforcement is improving but limited. In 2025 the GGL reviewed 2,662 illegal gambling or advertising websites and removed access to 1,843 (69%). Its tools are payment blocking (§9 GlüStV), app-store and search delisting, and prohibition orders; court rulings in Saxony-Anhalt have constrained ISP-level IP blocking [analyst reference, unverified]. The commercial implication: a licensed slots operator competes on trust, speed of payout and cross-sell from sports rather than on RTP or bonus value; a B2B studio needs a GGL-compliant game catalogue (€1 stake, 5-second cycle, no jackpot/autoplay) and LUGAS-ready platform integration to sell into the >60 licensed operators — a defensible niche precisely because global content is not plug-and-play here.

segments.name: Lottery, social lotteries and land-based (Spielbanken, gaming halls)
segments.headline: Three-quarters of the €14.4bn market is land-based and the state lottery monopoly supplies ~70% of the RennwLottG tax line; private access is limited to online brokerage and social-lottery distribution.
narrative: Land-based gambling generated €10.9bn (~$12.8bn) of the €14.4bn (~$16.8bn) regulated GGR in 2025 — about 75% — spanning gaming halls (Spielhallen, dominated by Gauselmann/Merkur and Novomatic/Löwen devices), the Land-concessioned Spielbanken, and the retail networks of the 16 state lottery companies in the Deutscher Lotto- und Totoblock. The segment is flat-to-declining as Land Spielhallen laws impose minimum distances and device caps, while online took the entire 2% of market growth. The state's wider take — €6.9bn (~$8.1bn) in 2025 across gambling taxes and levies including the Spielbankabgabe and lottery concession levies — explains the Länder's protective stance toward the lottery monopoly and their reluctance to loosen the online regime.

Lottery is the quiet giant of the tax statistics. Deducting the 5.3% stake taxes implied by GGL-reported sports, slots, poker and horse stakes from quarterly receipts leaves ~€429m (~$502m) in Q1-26 and ~€455m (~$532m) in Q2-26 attributable to lottery tax — 68–70% of the Rennwett- und Lotteriesteuer line, or ~€1.7bn annualised (derived estimate). The lottery tax is 20% of ticket price net of tax (≈16.7% of the gross ticket), so the implied gross lottery sales base is ~€10bn a year across Lotto 6aus49, Eurojackpot, class and social lotteries (estimate). Jackpot cycles, not operator behaviour, drive quarterly swings in this component.

The GGL Marktmonitor reports the privately accessible lottery slices separately. In Q1-26 class lotteries took €54m (~$63m) and social lotteries €328m (~$384m) in stakes (combined €382m), while commercial online lottery brokerage reached €258m (~$302m). Social lotteries (Deutsche Fernsehlotterie, Aktion Mensch and peers) produced €807m (~$944m) GGR in 2025 with their online portion up 11% to €444m (~$519m). Online brokerage is a licensed, low-margin intermediation business — ZEAL (Lotto24/Tipp24) reported 9M-26 revenue approaching €200m per trade press — and secondary 'bet-on-lottery' products are not permitted, which closed Germany to the Lottoland model.

For an operator weighing the market, the lottery and land-based segments are strategically relevant in two ways only: as the fiscal reason the regime will stay conservative, and as a brokerage/affiliate adjacency that is already consolidated. Land-based gaming-hall economics (municipal amusement tax plus VAT on top of device limits) and Spielbank concessions (Land tenders, levies that can exceed half of GGR) are closed or capital-intensive for a new entrant and sit outside B2Tech's online competence.

blocks.takeaway: Lottery and land-based matter only as the fiscal reason for a conservative regime and as an already-consolidated brokerage adjacency.

These segments sit outside B2Tech's online competence.

segments.name: Licensing, tax and enforcement regime
segments.headline: A centralised online licensing regime (GGL) layered on a federal turnover tax and 16 Land-level land-based regimes; the §32 evaluation due 31 Dec 2026 and the 2027 renewal cycle set the next rule-set.
narrative: The legal architecture has three tiers. The Interstate Treaty on Gambling 2021 (Glücksspielstaatsvertrag, in force 1 July 2021) sets product, player-protection and advertising rules and created the Gemeinsame Glücksspielbehörde der Länder in Halle (Saale), which has held full competence for online sports betting, virtual slots, online poker and lottery brokerage since 1 January 2023 and is funded by the Länder; the Rennwett- und Lotteriegesetz (federal) sets the taxes, whose revenue accrues to the Länder; and Land law governs Spielbanken, gaming halls, retail betting shops and — under §22c — any online table-game licences. The treaty runs to 31 December 2028 with automatic extension unless terminated, and §32 obliges the Länder to evaluate its effects by 31 December 2026 [treaty provisions from analyst reference]. Christian Hochgrebe took the chair of the GGL Administrative Board on 1 July 2026; the executive board is Ronald Benter and Benjamin Schwanke.

Licence mechanics: applications are made to the GGL per product (sports betting, virtual slots, online poker, online lottery brokerage; social and class lotteries under separate provisions). Core conditions [analyst reference, not re-verified in session]: a security deposit of €5m (~$5.9m) that can be raised to €50m (~$58.5m) with stakes; EU-based servers and data access for the regulator; a safety concept; mandatory connection to LUGAS (limit and activity files) and OASIS (exclusion register); a German-language offer with segregated player accounts; an administrative fee calculated on projected annual stakes (§9a); and annual audited reporting. Licence duration and the fee tariff could not be verified here — the first virtual-slot and poker licences were issued in 2022, which implies a renewal wave from 2027 [unverified]. In 2025 LUGAS processed data from more than 60 licensed operators and roughly five million registered player accounts.

The tax regime is the market's defining feature and has not changed since 1 July 2021. Sports betting, virtual slots, online poker and horse-race betting are all taxed at 5.3% of stakes — a turnover base that is indifferent to margin, bonus cost or product mix — while lotteries pay 20% of ticket price net of tax. In cash terms this family of taxes delivered €2.46bn (~$2.88bn) in 2025 (−1%), €1,901m (~$2.22bn) in 9M-26 (~+4% implied) and €622.1m (~$728m) in Q3-26 (+11%); the BMF's official estimate for FY-26 is €2,510m (~$2.94bn, +1.9%). The Länder have no fiscal incentive to migrate to a GGR base: the turnover tax is simple, high-yielding and applies to unlicensed operators too, which is why industry lobbying for a GGR tax has gone nowhere in five years.

Enforcement combines prohibition orders, payment blocking (§9), app-store and search delisting, and co-operation with Land media authorities on advertising; ISP-level blocking has been constrained by Saxony-Anhalt administrative courts [analyst reference]. 2025 output: 2,662 illegal sites reviewed, 1,843 removed. Separately, retrospective litigation is a live liability for anyone who operated into Germany before July 2021 without a German licence: German courts have allowed players to reclaim losses from unlicensed operators, and the Federal Court of Justice referred the compatibility of such claims with EU law to the CJEU [status unverified] — an entrant with a legacy grey-market book should price this.

Direction of travel for 2027–28 (our view): the evaluation will document a stable licensed market with contested channelisation and will recommend incremental, not radical, change. Probable: modest relaxation of the €1 stake and €1,000 deposit mechanics for verified high-affordability players, extension of live-betting markets, stronger payment-blocking powers and influencer/affiliate rules, and encouragement — not a mandate — for more Länder to license table games. Improbable: a switch to GGR taxation or a nationwide live-casino licence. Any amendment requires all 16 Landtage, so the 2028 treaty expiry is the realistic implementation date.

segments.name: Payments, responsible gambling and advertising
segments.headline: Bank-rail payments, a €1,000/month cross-operator deposit cap enforced centrally through LUGAS, and a 06:00–21:00 ad ban for slots/poker make Germany the most friction-heavy large market in Europe for customer acquisition.
narrative: Payments are conventional and fully traceable. Licensed sites accept SEPA transfers, Sofort/Klarna, PayPal, paysafecard and debit/credit cards; crypto is not accepted, operators may not extend credit, and every deposit is checked against the player's cross-operator monthly limit in the LUGAS limit file before it is accepted. The default cap is €1,000 (~$1,170) per month across all licensed operators, raisable on proof of means to €10,000 and, for a small share of players, €30,000 [thresholds from analyst reference]. The GGL can direct payment-service providers to stop processing for unlicensed operators under §9 GlüStV, which — with app-store and search delisting — is now its principal enforcement lever. For an operator the practical consequence is high KYC-at-registration friction and a hard ceiling on VIP economics; offshore sites' absence of these frictions is the main driver of leakage in casino.

Responsible-gambling architecture is centralised rather than operator-led. LUGAS (run on Dataport infrastructure) maintains the limit file and an activity file that prevents simultaneous play with more than one licensed operator; OASIS is the nationwide self- and third-party exclusion register with a minimum exclusion period; a one-click 'panic button' triggers a 24-hour lockout; virtual slots carry the €1 (~$1.17) stake cap, ≥5-second spin, no autoplay and no jackpots; and operators must deploy early-detection systems and periodic reality checks [rules from analyst reference]. In 2025 the system covered >60 operators and ~5m registered accounts. These are compliance costs, but they also neutralise the UK-style affordability debate: Germany already has the hardest limits in Western Europe, which lowers the probability of further tightening in the 2026 evaluation and marginally raises the probability of selective loosening.

Advertising is permitted but tightly ring-fenced. Broadcast and online advertising for virtual slots, online poker and online casino is banned between 06:00 and 21:00; advertising may not target minors or vulnerable groups; sports-betting advertising may not feature active athletes or officials and may not run immediately before or during live sports broadcasts for bets on that event; the GGL's advertising guidance restricts influencer/streamer promotion and bonus messaging [GlüStV §5 and GGL guidance, analyst reference]. Sports sponsorship remains the dominant above-the-line channel, which again favours incumbents with existing Bundesliga and club deals. For B2Tech, the practical acquisition toolkit is search/affiliate (within GGL affiliate rules), post-21:00 TV and streaming, and sports sponsorship — all of which are priced for scale players.

Net commercial reading: the combination of a deposit cap, no parallel play, a stake cap and daytime ad bans compresses both ARPU and acquisition efficiency, so unit economics only work with low CAC (organic brand or cross-sell from sports) and a low cost base. It also means product differentiation is constrained to UX, payout speed, odds and content curation within the €1/5-second envelope — areas where a technology-led entrant can compete, but not with a bonus-driven playbook.

highlights.text: Scale with stability: €14.4bn (~$16.8bn) regulated GGR, €2.46bn (~$2.88bn) of RennwLottG tax from licensed operators, a treaty fixed to end-2028 and a single national online regulator — the rules will not swing on a single election.
Online stakes are compounding faster than the flat GGR headline: Q1-26 total stakes +9.4% (online +10.0%), virtual slots +9.3% and sequentially up in Q2; slots GGR +11% in 2025 to €543m (~$635m).
Event elasticity is proven: Q3-26 tax +11% with July +26% on World Cup 2026 betting — a licensed sportsbook with live content captures tournament demand at scale.

The §32 evaluation (due 31 Dec 2026) is the first formal window since 2021 to loosen the €1 stake, €1,000 deposit mechanics and live-betting catalogue — the regime is already at the tight end, so the skew of change is toward selective relaxation.
Retail-to-online migration continues (retail sports share 25.6% → 23.0% in one quarter), expanding the digital pool without new regulation.
Sports-betting channelisation is high and reported hold is rich (22.8% on GGL definitions): a licensed sportsbook is the credible front door and cross-sell base for slots and poker.

B2B opportunity: content and platform must be GGL-specific (€1 stake, 5-second cycle, LUGAS/OASIS integration) — global catalogues are not plug-and-play, creating a defensible supply niche into >60 licensed operators.

lowlights.text: Turnover tax: 5.3% of stakes on sports, slots, poker and horse betting is ~45% of GGR for slots at an 11.8% hold and ~23–30% for sports — payable on losing months and before bonus cost. No change proposed; the Länder's fiscal interest runs the other way.

Product handicap versus offshore: €1 stake, 5-second spin, no jackpots/autoplay/live casino, €1,000 cross-operator deposit cap, no parallel play — the stated reason unlicensed share is 23% of online play (Mar-26 study) and, by industry estimates, 70–80% of casino/slot activity.
Online table games and live casino are not federally licensable; access is Land-by-Land with small, tender-based licence counts (SH live; NRW [unverified]).

Governance: any treaty amendment needs all 16 Landtage, and €6.9bn (~$8.1bn) of state levies anchored in the lottery monopoly make the Länder conservative — expect incremental change in 2028, not a liberalised regime in 2027.
Q3 headline growth is flattered: September implied ~€194m (~$227m), ~−3% YoY; underlying ex-World Cup growth is low-to-mid single digit and online poker stakes are down 11–15%.

Legacy liability: player-reimbursement claims against operators that took German business pre-2021 without a German licence remain live in the courts (BGH/CJEU track, status unverified) — relevant to any partner or acquisition target.

Data opacity: no official operator shares, the GGL Q3-26 Marktmonitor is not yet out, and the Destatis product split of the €622.1m was not retrievable — several figures in this brief are derived and flagged as such.

forecast.intro: The official bridge is the BMF's 2026 estimate for the Rennwett- und Lotteriesteuer family — €2,510m (~$2.94bn), +1.9% on FY-25's €2,460m (~$2.88bn) — against a 9M-26 actual of €1,901m (~$2.22bn), ~+4% implied. Q3's +€61.6m (~$72m) was driven by sports betting (World Cup timing) and virtual slots (+9–10% stakes), partly offset by online poker (stakes −11% to −15%) and a flat lottery base. Q4 needs only ~€609m (−4% YoY) to meet the BMF number; on a flat Q4 (~€636m implied for Q4-25) FY-26 lands at ~€2.54bn (~$2.97bn), and with modest slots growth ~€2.54–2.57bn (+3–4%) — our estimate, not an official figure.
forecast.view: **Market:** we expect regulated online GGR to grow 3–5% a year through 2027 (estimate) — slots high single digit, sports betting mid single digit ex-tournaments, poker negative — with stakes growing faster than GGR as the €1/5-second format keeps hold low; land-based flat to −2%. Online penetration drifts from ~24% toward ~26–27% by 2027 (estimate). **Tax:** the 5.3% turnover base stays; no Land has a reason to give up a tax that also captures unlicensed operators. Receipts track stakes, so FY-27 receipts ~+2–4% absent a tournament (estimate). **Rules:** the §32 evaluation (due 31 Dec 2026) will frame a GlüStV amendment package for 2027 negotiation and 2028 implementation: likely selective relaxation of deposit-raise procedures and live-betting markets, tighter affiliate/influencer and payment-blocking provisions, and a nudge toward more Land table-game licences; unlikely a GGR tax or federal live casino. **Enforcement** intensifies on payments and app stores rather than ISP blocking. **Leverage/entry:** for B2Tech, the risk-adjusted path is B2B supply first (GGL-compliant content, LUGAS-ready platform) and, if B2C, a sportsbook-led entry timed to the 2027 renewal window with slots as cross-sell; retail and table games are not where to deploy capital.
watch: GGL Q3-26 Marktmonitor (expected Nov 2026): size of the World Cup sports-stake spike and whether slots stakes stayed >€1.2bn/quarter.
Destatis/BMF product-level split of the €622.1m and the October/November monthly prints — confirms whether September's implied ~−3% is a trend or rounding.
§32 GlüStV evaluation report (due 31 Dec 2026) and the Minister-Presidents' conference response in H1-27 — the agenda on stake/deposit limits, live betting, table games and tax base.
2027 renewal cycle for the first virtual-slot and poker licences [timing unverified] — fee tariff, security-deposit scaling and any new conditions.
